frames.caption: Ten people, ten heights in centimetres, all example values. Each dot is one sample, and the letter x names a sample, so yours is x = 173 cm.
Count the heights in bins and the pile shows its shape. The mean is the average height, and the variance is the average squared distance from that mean.
Drag μ to slide the bell and σ to widen it. The score adds the log of the bell's height over each of the 10 dots, so a bell that stands tall over every dot scores best.
Call the best bell p(x). Its height is measured per centimetre, so it is a density, telling how thickly heights pile up near x, and never a chance on its own.
The chance of landing in a range is the area under p over that range. A narrow strip has area close to height times width, so one exact height has area zero.
Fix μ and let x move, and the formula is a density over heights. Fix your height at 173 and let μ move, and the same formula is a likelihood, scoring each possible centre.
Likelihood multiplies p at every sample, so one badly covered dot drags the whole product down. Taking the log turns the product of ten into a sum of ten.
Slide μ until the tangent on the score lies flat. The slope is the sum of the ten distances xᵢ − μ, so it is zero exactly where μ is the average height.
Now slide σ with μ at the average. The tangent lies flat where σ² equals the average squared distance, the variance the pile gave, so fitting by likelihood returns the two summary numbers.
Score only your own 173 cm and every narrower bell scores higher, so the best fit is a spike of zero width. That is why fitting needs all ten heights.
Sweep from the far left, keeping a running total of the area under p. Call the running total F(x); it climbs from 0 to 1, and its slope at any x is p(x).
Read F upwards and a height x gives a share F(x). Read the same curve from the side and a share u gives back a height F⁻¹(u), one sample from the bell.
Feed in many evenly spread random u's and the heights pile up in the bell's shape. All the randomness lives in u, and F⁻¹ is a fixed rule that only moves it.
